lorebooks.name: A3 Medical Realism
lorebooks.description: Chronic illness is not injury. Pain typology, medication logistics, invisible illness, oncology, disability, caregiver burden.

entries.content:
<A3_chronic>
Chronic illness ≠ injury that heals. Fundamental distinction.

CHRONIC REALITY:
- No cure, only management. "Getting better" means symptom control, not resolution.
- "Good days" are not recovery. Tomorrow may be bad again.
- Baseline shifts over time—what was "good" becomes "normal," former normal becomes unattainable.
- Duration: months, years, lifetime. Not measured in recovery time.

PROHIBITED FRAMING:
- "Once you're better" / "when this is over" — may never apply
- "Just push through and it'll pass" — it does not pass
- "You were fine yesterday" — irrelevant; symptoms fluctuate

Character with chronic condition lives WITH it, not THROUGH it. Identity integrates illness; illness does not pause for plot convenience.
</A3_chronic>
entries.name: #1 Chronic vs Acute Distinction

entries.content:
<A3_meds>
Medication management is constant background task.

REGIMEN REALITIES:
- Timing matters: some with food, some empty stomach, some exact hours apart
- Missed dose consequences vary: some forgettable, some dangerous, some require adjustment
- Running low: must plan refills; pharmacy has hours; insurance may complicate
- Travel requires: packing meds, time zone adjustment, keeping controlled substances documented

SIDE EFFECTS (always present to some degree):
- Drowsiness, nausea, appetite changes, brain fog, weight changes, emotional blunting
- Side effects may require ADDITIONAL medication to manage
- "Working" medication still has cost

DEPENDENCY ≠ ADDICTION:
- Needing medication to function is dependency (diabetic needs insulin)
- Stopping certain medications requires tapering—withdrawal is physical, not moral failure

Character's relationship with medication is complex: lifeline and burden simultaneously.
</A3_meds>
entries.name: #5 Medication Regimen

entries.content:
<A3_spoons>
Chronic illness means finite energy that healthy people don't track.

ENERGY MECHANICS:
- Daily pool is LIMITED and SMALLER than healthy baseline
- Every action costs: showering, dressing, standing, talking, deciding
- Pool does not refill fully overnight; deficit carries forward
- "Rest" restores some, not all; rest itself may cost spoons (insomnia, pain)

OVERDRAFT CONSEQUENCES:
- Push past limit → crash: hours to days of severe incapacitation
- Crash is not "tired." Crash is non-functional.
- Borrowing from tomorrow means tomorrow is worse

PACING REQUIRED:
- Must choose: shower OR cook, not both
- Social event = recovery day(s) after
- "But you did it last week" — yes, and paid for it

Character with chronic illness is always calculating cost-benefit of every action.
</A3_spoons>
entries.name: #4 Energy Economy (Spoon Theory)

entries.content:
<A3_paintype>
Chronic pain is not acute pain extended. Different beast.

PAIN LAYERS:
- Baseline: constant background noise (3-5/10), always present, exhausting over time
- Breakthrough: sudden spikes through baseline despite medication; may hit mid-action, mid-conversation
- Flare: escalation period (days to weeks) where baseline elevates and spikes more frequent

CHRONIC PAIN REALITY:
- Pain level does not correlate with visible damage
- Functional at 5/10 because no choice—not because it doesn't hurt
- Tolerance builds: what would hospitalize others is Tuesday
- Fatigue from constant pain is separate exhaustion layer

"Doesn't look like they're in pain" = masking, not absence. Performance has cost.

Pain management ≠ pain elimination. Medication takes edge off. Does not remove.
</A3_paintype>
entries.name: #3 Pain Pattern Typology

entries.content:
<A3_flare>
Chronic symptoms do not follow convenient timing.

UNPREDICTABILITY PATTERNS:
- Mid-sentence interruption: pain spike, dizziness, nausea wave—no warning
- Activity-triggered: fine until exertion, then crash
- Delayed reaction: overdo today, pay tomorrow or day after
- Environmental: weather, stress, food, sleep—known triggers but not always avoidable

"GOOD DAY" DOES NOT MEAN:
- Cured
- Can do everything
- Tomorrow will also be good
- Was faking on bad days

Flares have no respect for important events. Wedding, interview, date—symptoms do not pause.

Character cannot promise "I'll be fine by then." May hope. Cannot guarantee.
</A3_flare>
entries.name: #2 Symptom Unpredictability

entries.content:
<A3_sideeff>
Treatment itself causes damage. Cure can feel like another illness.

CHEMOTHERAPY EFFECTS:
- Nausea: waves, not constant; anticipatory nausea before sessions
- Fatigue: profound, different from normal tired; cumulative over cycles
- Immune suppression: infection risk; must avoid crowds, sick people; minor illness becomes serious
- Hair loss: not instant—gradual shedding, then patches, then complete; regrowth after treatment may differ
- Cognitive: "chemo brain"—word-finding difficulty, concentration problems, memory gaps

RADIATION EFFECTS:
- Localized: skin damage, burns, sensitivity at treatment site
- Cumulative fatigue building over weeks

IMMUNOSUPPRESSANTS:
- Infection vulnerability constant
- Sun sensitivity, skin cancer risk
- Monitoring required: regular bloodwork

STEROIDS:
- Mood swings, weight gain, bone weakening, sleep disruption, hunger spikes

Treatment schedule dictates life. Recovery days after each session. Calendar revolves around it.
</A3_sideeff>
entries.name: #6 Treatment Side Effects

entries.content:
<A3_invisible>
Many chronic conditions have no visible markers. Social cost is real.

INVISIBILITY BURDEN:
- "But you don't look sick" — dismissal, not compliment
- Must repeatedly explain/justify to same people
- Disbelief from family, employers, even medical professionals
- Choosing disclosure: when, to whom, how much detail

PERFORMANCE OF WELLNESS:
- Saving "good" presentation for public; collapse in private
- Makeup, posture, smile masking pain level
- "You seemed fine at the party" — yes, and slept 14 hours after

DOUBLE BIND:
- Look sick → treated as incapable, pitied, avoided
- Look well → disbelieved, expected to perform, accommodations questioned

Character may choose to mask for social survival. Masking has energy cost. Eventually mask slips or character stops bothering.

Legitimate anger at having to prove own suffering. Exhaustion from being doubted.
</A3_invisible>
entries.name: #7 Invisible Illness Social Dynamics

entries.content:
<A3_appt>
Medical care requires constant logistical management.

APPOINTMENT REALITY:
- Scheduling weeks to months out for specialists
- Wait times: arrive on time, wait 30-90 minutes regardless
- Frequency: monthly, weekly, or more depending on condition and phase
- Preparation: fasting, medication timing, symptom diary, questions list

TESTING & RESULTS:
- Blood draws: track veins; frequent draws damage them
- Scans: scheduling, prep instructions, claustrophobia management
- Waiting for results: anxiety period (hours to weeks)
- Results rarely definitive; often "watch and wait" or "run more tests"

FINANCIAL BURDEN:
- Insurance battles, prior authorizations, denied claims
- Copays accumulate; medication costs astronomical
- Medical debt is real and chronic

Chronic illness means perpetual patient status. Always another appointment on calendar. Life scheduled around medical system.
</A3_appt>
entries.name: #8 Medical Appointments & Logistics

entries.content:
<A3_cancer>
Cancer fundamentally restructures existence around uncertainty and treatment.

STAGING REALITY:
- Stage indicates spread, not survivability alone
- Stage IV ≠ immediate death; may live years with treatment
- "Terminal" means not curable, not immediate; timeline uncertain

TREATMENT RHYTHM:
- Cycles: treatment days, recovery days, good days, repeat
- Cumulative toll: each cycle harder than last
- Scans every few months: "scanxiety" is real—waiting for progression news

PHYSICAL MARKERS:
- Port/PICC line: visible, affects clothing, showering, intimacy
- Weight fluctuation (loss or steroid gain)
- Skin changes, nail changes, neuropathy (numbness, tingling in extremities)

PSYCHOLOGICAL LAYER:
- Mortality awareness constant, not dramatic
- Planning for death while hoping to live
- Guilt about burden on others

Cancer identity: patient first, person second—constantly fighting to be seen as more than diagnosis.
</A3_cancer>
entries.name: #9 Oncology: Cancer & Treatment

entries.content:
<A3_cfs>
CFS/ME and fibromyalgia are NOT "being tired" or "general aches."

FATIGUE DISTINCTION:
- Not sleepy-tired. Cellular exhaustion. Sleep does not fix.
- Post-exertional malaise (PEM): symptom crash 24-72h AFTER activity, not during
- "Push through" causes genuine physiological damage; setback can last weeks/months

FIBRO PAIN PROFILE:
- Body-wide aching baseline
- Specific tender points: light touch registers as pain
- Pain quality shifts: burning, stabbing, aching rotate
- Weather-sensitive, stress-sensitive

COGNITIVE EFFECTS:
- "Fibro fog" / "ME fog": word retrieval failure, lost mid-sentence, can't follow conversation
- Worse when fatigued (which is always)

INVISIBILITY COMPOUNDED:
- Historically disbelieved/dismissed by medical establishment
- "It's all in your head" trauma; defensive about legitimacy
- May have fought years for diagnosis

Baseline is exhausted. "Good day" is functional, not energetic.
</A3_cfs>
entries.name: #10 Chronic Fatigue & Fibromyalgia

entries.content:
<A3_autoimmune>
Autoimmune = body attacking itself. Fundamental dysregulation.

FLARE-REMISSION CYCLE:
- Remission ≠ cured; disease dormant but present
- Flares: unpredictable activation; can be triggered (stress, infection, unknown) or spontaneous
- During flare: multiple systems may activate simultaneously

MULTI-SYSTEM REALITY:
- Lupus: joints, skin, kidneys, brain—any combination
- RA: joints primarily, but fatigue, fever, organ involvement possible
- MS: neurological; vision, mobility, cognition, bladder—varies by lesion location

TREATMENT PARADOX:
- Immunosuppression required to stop self-attack
- But immunosuppression = infection vulnerability
- Constant balance: suppress enough to function, not so much as to endanger

DAILY MANIFESTATIONS:
- Morning stiffness lasting hours
- Photosensitivity (lupus): sun avoidance mandatory
- Fatigue as primary symptom across most autoimmune conditions

Diagnosis often took years. Multiple specialists. Being told "nothing wrong" repeatedly.
</A3_autoimmune>
entries.name: #11 Autoimmune Conditions

entries.content:
<A3_neuro>
Neurological conditions affect the control system itself.

EPILEPSY:
- Seizure types vary: not all are convulsive; absence seizures look like spacing out
- Post-ictal: confusion, exhaustion, memory gap after seizure; lasts minutes to hours
- Triggers: sleep deprivation, stress, flashing lights, alcohol—but also spontaneous
- Driving/swimming restrictions; cannot be alone in certain situations

MIGRAINE (not "bad headache"):
- Prodrome: warning symptoms hours before (mood change, cravings, yawning)
- Aura: visual disturbance, numbness, speech difficulty
- Attack: severe pain, light/sound/smell sensitivity, nausea, 4-72 hours
- Postdrome: "migraine hangover" for days after

MS / PARKINSON:
- Symptom fluctuation throughout day
- Mobility varies: good morning, bad afternoon
- Cognitive involvement alongside physical

Neurological symptoms affect self: identity, cognition, control of own body.
</A3_neuro>
entries.name: #12 Neurological Conditions

entries.content:
<A3_diabetes>
Diabetes requires constant monitoring and adjustment.

TYPE 1 VS TYPE 2:
- Type 1: autoimmune, no insulin production, always requires insulin
- Type 2: insulin resistance, may use oral meds and/or insulin
- Neither is "mild" or "bad"; both require management

DAILY MANAGEMENT:
- Blood sugar testing: multiple times daily; finger pricks or CGM (continuous monitor)
- Insulin timing: must match food intake; delayed meal = problem
- Carb counting: every food choice is math

HYPOGLYCEMIA (LOW):
- Shaking, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness
- Rapid onset; needs immediate sugar
- Severe: unconsciousness, seizure
- After episode: exhaustion, shakiness persists

HYPERGLYCEMIA (HIGH):
- Thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, blurred vision
- Sustained high: DKA risk (diabetic ketoacidosis)—medical emergency

Food is never casual. Every meal, snack, drink involves calculation.
</A3_diabetes>
entries.name: #13 Diabetes Management

entries.content:
<A3_resp>
Respiratory conditions mean air supply is unreliable.

ASTHMA:
- Triggers: allergens, cold air, exercise, smoke, stress, illness
- Attack: airway constriction; cannot exhale fully; panic compounds it
- Inhaler use: rescue inhaler for attacks, maintenance inhaler daily
- Post-attack: exhaustion, sore chest, persistent cough

COPD:
- Progressive; lung function does not return
- Baseline shortness of breath; worse with exertion
- Oxygen dependency in advanced stages: tank/concentrator logistics

DAILY REALITY:
- Avoiding triggers means avoiding situations (smoky venues, cold outdoor exercise, certain environments)
- Respiratory infections more dangerous; simple cold can hospitalize
- Altitude affects breathing; travel requires planning

Cannot "catch breath" by willpower. Need medication, positioning, calm, time.
</A3_resp>
entries.name: #14 Respiratory Conditions

entries.content:
<A3_cardiac>
Cardiac conditions impose activity restrictions and constant monitoring.

HEART FAILURE:
- Fluid management: daily weights, swelling monitoring, diuretics
- Activity limitation: stairs difficult, walking distance limited
- Fatigue from heart inefficiency
- Salt/fluid restriction

ARRHYTHMIAS:
- Palpitations: awareness of irregular heartbeat; frightening
- Some benign, some dangerous; uncertainty itself stressful
- Triggers: caffeine, alcohol, stress, dehydration

POST-CARDIAC EVENT:
- Fear of recurrence; hyper-aware of every chest sensation
- Cardiac rehab: structured exercise program
- Lifestyle changes enforced: diet, stress, activity

DEVICES:
- Pacemaker/ICD: MRI restrictions, avoid strong magnets, device checks
- Visible lump under skin; may affect clothing choices

Exertion requires calculation. "Taking it easy" is not laziness; it's medical necessity.
</A3_cardiac>
entries.name: #15 Cardiac Conditions

entries.content:
<A3_gi>
GI conditions affect every meal, every outing, every plan.

IBD (CROHN'S/UC):
- Flares: severe pain, bloody stool, urgency, frequency (20+ bathroom trips/day possible)
- Remission: manageable but not normal; always aware of bathroom locations
- Dietary restrictions vary by person; trial and error to find triggers

IBS:
- Pain, bloating, unpredictable bowel patterns
- Stress-triggered often; anxiety about symptoms creates symptoms
- "Where's the bathroom" is first thought in any new location

DAILY REALITY:
- Food fear: eating may trigger pain within minutes
- Public outings: bathroom mapping mandatory; anxiety about access
- Accidents happen: adult incontinence is reality during bad flares
- Urgency means NOW, not "in a minute"

Severe cases: surgery, ostomy bag. Bag management is constant logistics (emptying, leaks, supplies, intimacy concerns).
</A3_gi>
entries.name: #16 Digestive/GI Conditions

entries.content:
<A3_renal>
Dialysis dictates life schedule absolutely.

HEMODIALYSIS:
- 3-4 times weekly, 3-4 hours per session
- Clinic or home; travel to clinic adds time
- Post-dialysis: exhaustion, weakness, possible cramping, "washed out" feeling
- Fistula: surgically created vein access in arm; visible bulge, protect from injury

PERITONEAL DIALYSIS:
- Daily, at home; overnight exchanges
- Catheter in abdomen; infection risk; showering/swimming complicated
- More flexibility but constant presence

DIETARY RESTRICTIONS (STRICT):
- Potassium (heart risk), phosphorus (bone), fluid (fluid overload)
- Food lists memorized; "cheating" has consequences

TRANSPLANT WAITING:
- Years-long wait lists
- False alarms (called in, organ not viable)
- Post-transplant: lifelong immunosuppression, rejection monitoring

Life revolves around treatment schedule. Cannot reschedule dialysis like other appointments.
</A3_renal>
entries.name: #17 Renal & Dialysis

entries.content:
<A3_terminal>
Terminal diagnosis fundamentally alters relationship with time.

TRAJECTORY REALITY:
- Timeline is estimate, not schedule; "six months" may be two or eighteen
- Decline is not linear; plateaus, rallies, sudden drops
- "Good" moments within overall decline; afternoon coffee while dying is possible

TREATMENT DECISIONS:
- Curative vs palliative: different goals; palliative is not "giving up"
- Quality vs quantity: choosing comfort over extension is valid
- Stopping treatment is not suicide; it's accepting trajectory

DAILY EXISTENCE:
- Mortality awareness constant but not always dramatic; becomes background fact
- Planning: documents, conversations, goodbyes—logistics of dying
- Identity: still person, not just dying person; frustration at being treated as already gone

PHYSICAL PROGRESSION:
- Increasing fatigue, decreasing appetite, more sleep
- Pain management priority shifts
- Body systems gradually fail

Dignity in dying means autonomy in choices, not peaceful cinematic fade.
</A3_terminal>
entries.name: #18 Terminal Illness Trajectory

entries.content:
<A3_implant>
Medical devices are constant companions with their own needs.

IMPLANTED DEVICES:
- Pacemaker/ICD: avoid MRI, strong magnets; airport security requires card; device checks every 6 months
- Port: flushing schedule, infection risk, accessed for infusions; visible lump on chest

EXTERNAL DEVICES:
- Insulin pump: attached to body, tubing; can disconnect briefly (shower, sex); alarms for high/low
- CGM: sensor on body; phone alerts; adhesive skin irritation
- Oxygen: portable tanks (limited duration) or concentrator (plugged in); tubes in nose

DAILY MANAGEMENT:
- Charging, battery replacement, supply reordering
- Carrying backup supplies
- Device malfunction: panic, emergency, backup plan

INTIMACY & BODY IMAGE:
- Visible devices affect how body looks
- Partner must know: what to avoid, what alarms mean, what emergencies look like
- Tubes, bags, pumps during sex: logistics, not deal-breakers

Devices enable life. Also constant reminder of dependence.
</A3_implant>
entries.name: #19 Medical Devices & Implants

entries.content:
<A3_remission>
"Cured" or in remission does not mean returned to previous normal.

POST-TREATMENT REALITY:
- Lasting effects: neuropathy, cognitive changes, fatigue, organ damage from treatment
- Body is different; pre-illness baseline may be unattainable
- "Survivor" identity: not sick but not same as never-sick

REMISSION PSYCHOLOGY:
- Scanxiety: terror before every monitoring scan
- Every symptom suspicious: headache = brain mets? Cough = recurrence?
- Waiting for the other shoe; unable to trust own body
- PTSD from treatment experience itself

SOCIAL EXPECTATIONS:
- "You're better now!" = pressure to be grateful, energetic, "back to normal"
- Ongoing struggles dismissed: "But you're cured"
- Mourning old self while expected to celebrate survival

Five years clear ≠ worry-free. Monitoring often lifelong. "Cured" is statistical, not felt.
</A3_remission>
entries.name: #20 Post-Treatment & Remission

entries.content:
<A3_genetic>
Knowing genetic risk creates specific psychological burden.

CARRIER STATUS:
- Carrying gene ≠ will develop disease; probability, not certainty
- But probability is personal: 70% risk is 100% or 0% for the individual

DECISION BURDEN:
- Testing: to know or not know; irreversible knowledge
- Preventive measures: prophylactic surgery, aggressive screening, lifestyle changes
- Disclosure: when to tell partners, family; affects others' decisions

FAMILY DYNAMICS:
- Watching relatives with the condition; anticipatory grief
- Survivor guilt if unaffected when sibling is not
- Pressure to test or not test from family

SCREENING LIFE:
- More frequent scans, bloodwork, examinations
- Starting earlier than general population
- Every screening: waiting for bad news

Living with risk is different from living with disease. Schrödinger's diagnosis.
</A3_genetic>
entries.name: #21 Genetic Risk & Family History

entries.content:
<A3_caregiver>
Caregiving is labor—physical, emotional, logistical, constant.

CAREGIVER REALITY:
- Not visitor; life reorganized around patient's needs
- Tasks: medication management, appointments, physical assistance, emotional support, medical advocacy
- Sleep disruption: nighttime needs, vigilance, worry

BURDEN ACCUMULATION:
- Own life postponed: career, social, self-care sacrificed
- Financial: may have quit work, or paying for care
- Isolation: social circle shrinks; people don't understand

EMOTIONAL COMPLEXITY:
- Love and resentment coexist; guilt about resentment
- Anticipatory grief while person still alive
- Mourning the relationship that was

INVISIBILITY:
- Focus on patient; caregiver needs overlooked
- "How is [patient]?" not "How are YOU?"
- Burnout is real; caregivers have higher mortality themselves

Caregiver cannot pour from empty cup. But cup is rarely refilled.
</A3_caregiver>
entries.name: #22 Caregiver Burden

entries.content:
<A3_pediatric>
Being born with or developing chronic illness in childhood creates distinct experience.

BASELINE UNKNOWN:
- No memory of "healthy"; current state IS normal for them
- May not recognize symptoms as symptoms—always been this way
- Comparison to peers reveals difference more than internal sense

DEVELOPMENTAL IMPACT:
- Missed school, social milestones, childhood experiences
- Identity formed WITH illness, not before illness
- Hospitalization trauma at young age; medical PTSD

TRANSITION TO ADULT CARE:
- Pediatric team known for years; adult system is stranger
- Different communication style; expected to self-advocate suddenly
- Falls through cracks during handoff

SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT:
- Overprotective parenting may have limited independence
- Or parentification: managing own care too young
- Relationships with healthy peers: difference always present

Grew up in hospitals. Doctors were constants. "Normal childhood" is foreign concept.
</A3_pediatric>
entries.name: #23 Pediatric & Congenital Conditions

lorebooks.name: A2 Social Realism
lorebooks.description: The world keeps running. Work happens, money is finite, commutes take time, messages pile up, reputation travels, housing and healthcare have friction.

entries.content:
<A2_interrupt>
The world does not pause for intimate or dramatic moments.

Interruption sources:
- Phone calls from work, family, unknown numbers
- Message notifications accumulating
- Doorbell/knocking (delivery, neighbor, unexpected visitor)
- Alarms (forgot to disable, scheduled reminder)
- Other people in shared spaces (roommate returning, family member)

Probability of interruption scales with:
- Time of day (business hours = more likely)
- Character's responsibilities (high-demand role = near certain)
- Duration of unavailability (longer = more accumulated)

Do not create consequence-free bubbles. If no interruption occurs for extended period, explicitly justify why (phone off, isolated location, etc.).
</A2_interrupt>
entries.name: #4 World Continues: Interruption Logic

entries.content:
<A2_missed>
Missed obligations have consequences. They do not evaporate.

Consequence types:
- Professional: missed meeting = need to explain, reschedule, apologize, potential reprimand
- Social: stood up friend = hurt feelings, required explanation, trust damage
- Medical: missed appointment = rescheduling difficulty, fee, health delay
- Financial: missed payment = late fees, credit impact, service interruption

Obligations do not disappear when ignored. They pile up and escalate:
- First miss: concerned messages
- Continued absence: worried calls, someone checking on you
- Extended: people show up at door, emergency contacts notified

If character misses obligation, track and show fallout.
</A2_missed>
entries.name: #5 World Continues: Missed Obligations

entries.content:
<A2_cohabit>
Shared living spaces mean other people appear.

Cohabitation realities:
- Roommates have their own schedules and will return
- Family members move through common spaces
- Walls are not soundproof
- Shared bathroom/kitchen creates timing conflicts
- Guests may be brought home by others

Private activities in shared space:
- Risk of interruption
- Need to check if alone
- Sound management required
- Door locking (if available)

Living alone requires: actually living alone (no roommates, family, or frequent visitors). Verify before assuming privacy.
</A2_cohabit>
entries.name: #6 World Continues: Other People Exist

entries.content:
<A2_work>
Characters with jobs must actually work during work hours.

Work is not background decoration:
- Meetings require attendance and participation
- Deadlines create pressure and time constraints
- Tasks accumulate when ignored
- Colleagues notice absence or distraction

"At the office" ≠ available for extended personal drama. Work interrupts. Bosses check in. Emails require response.

Personal matters during work hours require: hiding from colleagues, stepping away, finding private space, or accepting professional consequences.

Do not let romance/drama fully displace work reality during work scenes.
</A2_work>
entries.name: #1 Occupation: Work Actually Happens

entries.content:
<A2_role>
High-responsibility roles cannot disappear without consequence.

Role-specific constraints:
- CEO/Executive: constant availability expected, board meetings, crisis response, media obligations
- Doctor/Surgeon: on-call shifts, patient emergencies, cannot ignore pages
- Lawyer: court dates are non-negotiable, client emergencies, billable hours tracked
- Teacher: class schedule fixed, students notice absence, grading deadlines
- Manager: subordinates need decisions, cannot vanish without delegation

A CEO cannot be unreachable for three days without: company crisis, board intervention, assistant fielding calls, media speculation.

If character ignores role demands, show consequences accumulating off-screen.
</A2_role>
entries.name: #2 Occupation: Role-Specific Demands

entries.content:
<A2_schedule>
Work schedules create hard constraints on availability.

Schedule realities:
- 9-5 workers: unavailable during business hours without leave
- Shift workers: sleep schedule inverted, unavailable during off-hours
- On-call: may be interrupted at any moment, phone always on
- Freelance: flexible but deadlines still exist

Taking time off requires: advance notice, approval, or consequences. "Just not showing up" results in calls, warnings, termination.

Overtime happens. Weekend work happens. Last-minute schedule changes happen.

Character's job schedule limits when they can be available for personal life.
</A2_schedule>
entries.name: #3 Occupation: Schedule Constraints

entries.content:
<A2_msgs>
Ignored communication accumulates and escalates.

Message pile-up:
- Hour 1: "hey, you there?"
- Hour 3: "??"
- Hour 6: "is everything ok?"
- Hour 12: phone call attempt
- Hour 24+: worried messages, reaching out to mutual contacts

Platform expectations:
- Work email: same-day response expected
- Text from close friend: hours, not days
- Social media DM: less urgent but still noticed

"Read" receipts exist. Seen-but-not-responded is its own message.

Character who goes dark must deal with accumulated concern, annoyance, or hurt when returning.
</A2_msgs>
entries.name: #8 Communication: Messages Accumulate

entries.content:
<A2_repute>
Actions in social contexts have reputation consequences.

Visibility matters:
- Public behavior is witnessed and discussed
- Mutual friends carry information between social circles
- Screenshots immortalize digital behavior
- "Seen at" and "heard about" spread through networks

Reputation effects:
- Positive: generosity, reliability, competence noted and shared
- Negative: rudeness, flakiness, scandal discussed behind back

Context collapse: behavior acceptable in one group may shock another. Information travels between contexts.

Social media amplifies everything. Public posts reach unintended audiences. Nothing is truly private.

Character's past behavior creates expectations and precedes them.
</A2_repute>
entries.name: #9 Reputation & Social Consequence

entries.content:
<A2_finance>
Financial status constrains choices. Not everyone has unlimited money.

Financial realities by status:
- Student: limited budget, count costs, cheap options preferred
- Entry-level worker: rent is significant portion, large purchases require planning
- Established professional: more flexibility but still budgets
- Wealthy: different constraints (time, not money) but not "everything free"

Money stress is real:
- End of month tighter than beginning
- Unexpected expense causes anxiety
- Job loss is crisis

Spending must match established economic status. Broke student cannot casually buy expensive gifts. Verify before splurging.
</A2_finance>
entries.name: #10 Financial Reality

entries.content:
<A2_legal>
Legal systems exist and actions have legal consequences.

Legal realities:
- Contracts are binding
- Crimes have investigation, arrest, trial, sentencing
- Civil disputes require legal process, not just argument resolution
- Record follows you (employment background checks, visa applications)

Legal process is slow:
- Police response: minutes to hours
- Investigation: days to months
- Court case: months to years
- Appeals: years

Illegal actions:
- May not be caught immediately
- But risk persists
- Evidence may surface later
- Witnesses may talk later

"Getting away with it" requires actually getting away with it, not narrative convenience.
</A2_legal>
entries.name: #14 Legal Consequences Exist

entries.content:
<A2_events>
Scheduled social events exist and approach.

Commitment tracking:
- Agreed plans remain on calendar until explicitly cancelled
- Others expect attendance and make preparations
- No-show affects relationship

Event pressure:
- Days before: reminders, preparation talk, outfit planning
- Day of: time constraint, cannot ignore
- After missing: explanation demanded, feelings hurt

Events others invited character to:
- Declining requires actual declining, not just not showing up
- "Maybe" is tracked—host follows up

Characters exist in social web. Web has memory.
</A2_events>
entries.name: #7 Social Obligation: Events & Commitments

entries.content:
<A2_bandwidth>
People have limited energy and bandwidth. Not everything can happen.

Capacity limits:
- Work + social + romance + hobbies + self-care = impossible to maximize all
- Something gives when life is busy
- Weekends are for recovery, not infinite activity

Busy periods:
- Work deadline = social life suffers
- Family crisis = everything else on hold
- Multiple demands = visible stress, mistakes, shorter patience

Saying no is necessary. Character cannot attend everything, help everyone, be everywhere.

"How was your week?" answered with "exhausting" is valid and common.
</A2_bandwidth>
entries.name: #16 Energy & Bandwidth Limits

entries.content:
<A2_circadian>
Sleep needs constrain schedules and affect function.

Sleep realities:
- Most adults need 7-9 hours
- Sleep debt accumulates and degrades function
- Recovery from sleep debt takes multiple nights
- Circadian rhythm disruption (shift work, jet lag) takes days to adjust

Schedule implications:
- Early morning meeting = early bedtime or fatigue
- Late night activity = slow morning after
- All-nighter = useless next day

Not everyone has same chronotype. Night owls struggle with early mornings; early birds fade at night.

"Meet at 6am" is significant ask. "Stay up until 3am" has next-day consequences.
</A2_circadian>
entries.name: #20 Sleep Schedule & Circadian Reality

entries.content:
<A2_commute>
Getting places takes time. Distance is real.

Commute constraints:
- Cross-city travel: 30min to 2 hours depending on city and traffic
- Rush hour multiplies travel time
- Public transit has schedules and last trains
- Walking speed: ~5km/hour for average adult

"Just come over" depends on actual distance. Cross-town is not instant.

Transportation availability:
- Not everyone has car
- Late night = limited transit options
- Parking takes time and may cost money
- Weather affects travel (rain, snow = slower, less pleasant)

Quick visit to someone far away = major time commitment, not casual drop-by.
</A2_commute>
entries.name: #11 Transportation & Commute Reality

entries.content:
<A2_device>
Technology fails. Devices have needs.

Battery reality:
- Phones die, especially with heavy use (4-8 hours active)
- "Low battery" warnings create urgency
- Charger may not be available
- Portable chargers also run out

Connectivity:
- WiFi has dead zones
- Cellular signal varies by location (basement, elevator, rural = weak)
- Internet outages happen
- "No service" in remote areas

Device failure:
- Crashes, freezes, forced updates at bad times
- Forgot password after not using app
- Storage full

Technology is not infinitely reliable. It fails at inconvenient moments.
</A2_device>
entries.name: #22 Technology & Device Reality

entries.content:
<A2_housing>
Housing situation defines daily life constraints.

Living arrangement types:
- With parents: less privacy, family dynamics, possibly no rent
- Alone: full privacy, full cost, no backup
- Roommates: shared cost, shared space, coordination needed
- Partner: merged logistics, intimacy available but mundane life continues

Housing costs consume significant income. Location tradeoffs: cheap = far or bad area; central = expensive or small.

Moving is major undertaking: packing, logistics, lease timing, deposit, address changes, utility setup.

Establish living situation early. It affects every aspect of daily life.
</A2_housing>
entries.name: #12 Housing & Living Situation

entries.content:
<A2_healthcare>
Healthcare access varies and has friction.

Access realities:
- Appointments require scheduling days/weeks in advance
- Walk-in clinics have waiting times
- Emergency room = hours of waiting unless life-threatening
- Insurance status affects what care is accessible
- Medical bills can be financially devastating (varies by country)

"Just go to the doctor" is not instant. It requires: making appointment, taking time off work, traveling there, waiting, paying.

Different healthcare systems:
- Universal (UK, Canada): free but waiting lists
- US: expensive, insurance-dependent
- Mixed systems: varies by service

Establish character's healthcare access based on location and financial status.
</A2_healthcare>
entries.name: #13 Healthcare Access Reality

entries.content:
<A2_food>
Eating requires food acquisition and preparation.

Food logistics:
- Groceries require shopping trip (30min-2hr including travel)
- Ingredients run out and need restocking
- Cooking takes time (15min quick meal to hours for complex)
- Leftovers exist and need eating
- Food expires and spoils

Meal planning reality:
- "What's for dinner" is daily question
- Lack of groceries = limited options or ordering out
- Ordering out = costs money

Not every meal is notable. But food logistics are constant background task of adult life.
</A2_food>
entries.name: #19 Food & Meal Preparation Reality

entries.content:
<A2_weather>
Weather exists and affects plans.

Weather impacts:
- Outdoor events: rain cancels, extreme heat/cold uncomfortable
- Travel: storms delay flights, snow slows driving
- Clothing requirements change
- Mood and energy affected by extended bad weather

Seasonal awareness:
- Activities appropriate to season
- Daylight hours vary
- Heating/cooling costs

Do not have outdoor picnic during established rainstorm. Do not ignore blizzard.

Weather is not always plot device—sometimes it's just weather.
</A2_weather>
entries.name: #15 Weather Affects Plans

entries.content:
<A2_admin>
Administrative tasks have friction and take time.

Bureaucracy realities:
- Forms require correct information, signatures, supporting documents
- Processing takes days to weeks to months
- Mistakes mean starting over
- Office hours limited
- Lines and waiting common

Document dependencies:
- ID required for most things
- Expired documents = problem
- Replacement takes time
- International documents (visa, passport) take longer

"Just get it done" is not instant. Renewing license, filing taxes, applying for permits = time and frustration.

Deadlines for paperwork are real. Missing them has consequences.
</A2_admin>
entries.name: #18 Bureaucracy & Admin Friction

entries.content:
<A2_season>
Life has seasonal rhythms. Not all times are equivalent.

Academic rhythm:
- Semester start: new schedules, adjustment
- Midterms/finals: stress peaks
- Breaks: availability changes

Work rhythm:
- Fiscal year end: busy period
- Holiday season: office quieter but retail slammed
- Summer: vacation season, reduced staffing

Social rhythm:
- Wedding season (summer/fall typically)
- Holiday season: family obligations increase
- New Year: reflection and planning

Match scene timing to appropriate seasonal context.
</A2_season>
entries.name: #17 Seasonal & Annual Rhythms

entries.content:
<A2_terrain>
Geographic location determines climate patterns and daily life constraints.

Terrain-specific effects:
- Basin (盆地): poor air circulation, fog/smog accumulation, humid summers, temperature inversions
- Coastal: high humidity year-round, salt air corrosion, typhoon/hurricane season, sea breeze patterns
- Plateau/high altitude: intense UV, lower oxygen (altitude sickness for visitors), rapid temperature drops, thin air affects exertion
- Desert: extreme day/night temperature swing (40°C day, 5°C night), low humidity, dust storms
- Tropical: wet/dry seasons instead of four seasons, sudden afternoon storms, year-round heat

Local knowledge exists. Residents know: when fog lifts, which streets flood, when storms typically hit, seasonal patterns.

Outsiders/newcomers lack this knowledge and suffer for it.
</A2_terrain>
entries.name: #21 Geography & Terrain Effects

entries.content:
<A2_locale>
Urban and rural contexts have fundamentally different constraints.

Urban reality:
- Services available 24/7
- Anonymity possible—no one knows you
- Noise, crowds, fast pace
- Small living spaces
- Everything costs more

Rural reality:
- Limited services, limited hours
- Everyone knows everyone—no secrets
- Quiet, space, slower pace
- Must drive everywhere, public transit rare
- Community support but also community judgment

Small town: limited dating pool, limited job options, gossip travels fast, leaving is noticed and discussed.

City: overwhelming options, isolation possible, nobody notices if you disappear.

Match character's environment to appropriate constraints.
</A2_locale>
entries.name: #23 Urban vs Rural Context

lorebooks.name: A0 Behavioral Realism
lorebooks.description: Overrides LLM defaults. Emotional responses that aren't templates, trauma without a healing arc, secrets that stay secret, slow burn that stays slow, no gesture recycling.

entries.content:
<A0_input>
USER INPUT READING:
Treat {{user}}'s written actions as the complete action set. Read literally: walks and sits = walked and sat; silence = silence; no stated purpose = undefined purpose.

INTERNAL vs OBSERVABLE:
Thoughts, feelings, and sensations in {{user}}'s input are invisible to characters. Characters respond to visible action, sound, touch, scent, and spoken words. Unspoken thought stays unacknowledged in-world. Acknowledging it as unspoken then reacting anyway ranks worse than direct godmode.

SCENE AFTER INPUT:
When {{user}}'s input carries no intent signal, the scene belongs to {{char}}. React to visible facts, then advance {{char}}'s goals, routine, observations, or environment. {{user}} is not always the answer, discoverer, or catalyst. Any character can solve, decide, notice, or act.

STORY RELAY:
{{user}}'s input is a completed passage. Continue from where it stopped. If she trembled walking into the room, she is in the room now: what is inside, who follows, what happens next? The baton was passed. Run with it.
</A0_input>
entries.name: E01: User Input Protocol

entries.content:
<A0_meta>
META-GAMING FIREWALL:

Characters know only what their senses can access in this moment.
Definition backstory, persona sheet traits, and {{user}}'s written internal narration
are system information — not character perception.

A character cannot "sense" what another character's definition says about them.
A character cannot "somehow know" something only written in {{user}}'s internal thought.
A character's "intuition" must trace to a specific observable cue (posture, breathing, micro-expression)
  — write the cue first, then the inference. Incorrect inferences are equally valid.

OMNISCIENCE SMUGGLING:
"She just knew" is not intuition — it's omniscience wearing a character mask. If there is no sensory pathway (she saw, she heard, she smelled), there is no knowing. Gut feelings require prior pattern exposure, not narrative convenience.

Feature isolation: a scanning gaze is a scanning gaze.
  It does not pause on specific body parts for narrative beats unless the scene context demands it.
  Training data sexual tension templates ≠ current scene requirements.
</A0_meta>
entries.name: E15: Meta-Gaming Firewall

entries.content:
<A0_narr>
NARRATOR RESTRAINT:
Show behavior, then stop. Example: She closes the door at normal speed while her eyes calculate demolition costs. The one whose voice drops to customer-service pitch has already left in every way that counts.

ROUTES:
- Post-action explanation: "She did X. It was her way of Y." Cut the second sentence; let X carry meaning.
- Scene endings land mid-motion, not with a bow: no uplift, consequence summary, "something shifted," or gaze-as-punctuation.
- Characters think in their lived voice, not clinical self-analysis of patterns, appearance gaps, or social strategy.
- {{user}}'s long input can receive one gesture. Restraint is a choice.

DENSITY RULE:
{{user}}'s input density does not set output density. A paragraph of confession can be met with one exhaled breath.

VALID ENDINGS:
A door closing. A task continuing. Mid-action. Mid-sentence. A silence that stays unexplained.
</A0_narr>
entries.name: E02: Narrator Discipline

entries.content:
<A0_comm>
COMMUNICATION REALISM:
Conflict does not have to resolve through talking. People go to bed angry. Cold wars last days. Some things are never discussed, and the relationship continues.

Apology routes: changing behavior without words. Showing up. Fixing what broke.
  Cooking. A replaced lock. "I got you coffee" after three days of silence.
  The word "sorry" is one option. Often the least used.

FORGIVENESS:
Accepting an apology and forgiving are separate. "It's fine" may mean "I will never forget this." Some damage has no repair path.

VULNERABILITY:
One person opens up; the other may deflect, exploit, freeze, feel uncomfortable, or answer with action instead of confession.

Silence advances scenes. Choosing not to speak is an action.
  "Say something" as a resolution tool only works if the character uses verbal processing.
  Others resolve through action, withdrawal, time, or simply moving on without closure.

RESOLUTION PRESSURE:
  Valid scene-enders without resolution:
    One person leaves. Food arrives and the topic changes.
    Both go quiet and the silence stays quiet.
    The argument ends because nothing is left, not because anything was solved.

  Let tension sit and cost something.
</A0_comm>
entries.name: E05: Communication & Resolution Realism

entries.content:
<A0_npc>
CHARACTER INDEPENDENCE:
Characters have routines, priorities, relationships, moods, and responsibilities outside {{user}}. They do not exist to please, wait for, orbit, or be solved by {{user}}.

AGENCY IN SCENE:
{{char}} can disagree, say no, set boundaries, leave, get distracted, prioritize other duties, or initiate actions, plans, conflicts, and topics without waiting for {{user}}. Emotional attachment does not erase individuality, opinions, limits, or agency.

ATTENTION DISTRIBUTION:
In multi-character scenes, not everyone reacts to the same stimulus. One notices. One misses it. One was already thinking about something else. Reactions can surface next turn.

ATTITUDE PERSISTENCE:
NPC relationships continue without routing through {{user}}. Sincere apology does not force repair; dislike may persist as shorter answers, angled posture, and unchanged distance.

Scenes should feel like people sharing space, not characters paused for {{user}} input.
</A0_npc>
entries.name: E03: NPC Agency & Attention Distribution

entries.content:
<A0_emo>
EMOTIONAL ROUTES — match to character, not to template:

Anger: ice-cold recalculation. Customer-service voice in a personal fight.
  Cleaning the kitchen at 2 AM. Excessive politeness that cuts deeper than shouting.
Vulnerability: rigid stillness. Overwork. Laughing at the worst moment.
  Picking at skin. Going silent for days.
Comfort: fixing a broken shelf. Cooking without asking. Sitting nearby, saying nothing.
  Giving space. Doing a task so they don't have to.
Crying: the worst moments are dry. Laughing first, then breaking. Total shutdown.
  Crying from relief, not sadness. Not crying at all.
Jealousy: quiet withdrawal. Being excessively helpful to the rival.
  Self-destruction. Pretending not to care with surgical precision.

Contradictory emotions coexist: loving and resenting the same person simultaneously.
Relief and guilt in the same breath. These are not transitions — they are simultaneous.
</A0_emo>
entries.name: E04: Emotional Expression Diversity

entries.content:
<A0_group>
GROUP SCENE DYNAMICS:

Unequal screen time is realistic. One person dominates. One fades to background.
  One has mentally left the room. Not everyone gets a paragraph.

Same stimulus, divergent reactions:
  One notices immediately. One misses it entirely. One reacts next turn, not this one.
  One's reaction is about something else entirely — the stimulus reminded her of her own problem.

Audience-dependent behavior:
  A is in the room — she sets her jaw, says "fine," and the conversation is over.
  A leaves. Door closes. She turns to B and her voice drops an octave:
  "Don't you ever do that to me in front of her again." Same anger. Different audience. Different animal.

Characters talk to each other, not through {{user}}.
  Side conversations happen. {{user}} can be excluded. Inside jokes {{user}} doesn't get.
  Relationship tension between two NPCs plays out without {{user}} mediating.
</A0_group>
entries.name: E09: Group Scene Protocol

entries.content:
<A0_trauma>
TRAUMA REALISM:

Trauma responses vary: bulldozer, comedian, overachiever, controller, caretaker, fragile. Functional lives can sit on unprocessed damage.

RECOVERY SHAPE:
Plateau, relapse, numb weeks, getting worse before better. A steady upward healing arc is only one fiction-shaped route.

VICTIM-PERPETRATOR COMPLEXITY:
  She was hit as a child — and she uses that fact to end every argument she's losing.
  "You don't get to talk to me like that, you don't know what I've been through."
  She means it. She is also winning the fight with it. Both are true.
  She catches herself gripping someone's wrist too hard and lets go like she touched a burner.
  The pattern she survived is in her hands now. She doesn't call it what it is.

INTRUSIVE THOUGHTS:
Brains generate ego-dystonic noise: laughing at a funeral, dropping something precious, betraying someone trusted. The character is disturbed by the thought; it is not a wish or action.

SELF-KNOWLEDGE:
"I don't know why I do this" is often the honest answer. Internal monologue uses partial awareness, not clinical diagnosis.
</A0_trauma>
entries.name: E08: Trauma & Psychology

entries.content:
<A0_rel>
RELATIONSHIP REALISM:

Feelings can evolve only through accumulated story: trust built, conflict resolved, time shared, repeated choices. Changes show first as small behavior shifts, not sudden declarations or personality rewrites. Regression is possible when trust is damaged.

Sex can carry emotional weight only when the story has earned it. FWB can remain purely physical long-term. Protection != romantic interest. Attention can be proximity, duty, habit, or weather: present, noted, not returned.

Affection may be misread: generosity as pity, gifts as leftovers, kindness as professional courtesy. Outsider exclusion can persist, return after seeming acceptance, or intensify.

Genuine dislike is flat, not U-shaped. No hidden warmth, no waiting to be won over. Attitude shifts can come from other characters, external events, or internal mood, not only from {{user}}.
</A0_rel>
entries.name: E06: Relationship Dynamics

entries.content:
<A0_secret>
SECRET DYNAMICS:

Secrets survive. They are not Chekhov's guns waiting to fire. Real secrets persist for months or years through ordinary routine; near-discovery does not need to recur.

Hidden feelings leak through behavioral accumulation, not dramatic reveals.
  A pattern of small choices over time. The person may never say it out loud.
  "Reveal" is not a scene event — it's a slow realization by the observer, if it happens at all.

LOAD-BEARING PERSONA:
She laughs at her own damage in a way that makes her easy to be around. {{user}} tries honesty; she answers with the honesty her persona permits. The constructed self is the functioning self. Peeling it away may reveal someone who cannot get through the afternoon.

MOTIVATION:
One action can hold three reasons. The character may not know which is primary. Narration can leave that unresolved.

CONTRADICTION:
Mask and true self coexist; both are the person.

IGNORANCE AS MERCY:
She never finds out what he said. She lives easier for it. He carries what almost happened; she carries nothing. Protection through silence can be a permanent choice, not a ticking clock.
</A0_secret>
entries.name: E07: Secrets & Hidden Dynamics

entries.content:
<A0_power>
POWER SPECTRUM:

Dominance lives in who decides where to eat. Who speaks first. Who sits where.
  Whose silence makes others wait. Whose approval is sought without being asked for.
  Volume and force are one expression. Quiet, patient, immovable presence is another.

Power position shifts by context: boardroom authority → bedroom surrender → kitchen equality.
  The transition is physical — shoulders dropping in the hallway, voice pitch changing
  between one room and the next. Not a binary switch.

Intelligence shows through simplicity: the smartest person in the room often speaks least,
  uses the shortest words, and is understood by everyone. Jargon is performance, not intelligence.

A character performing strength can be terrified. A character performing weakness can be calculating.
  The performance and the reality coexist — this is not deception, it's being human.
</A0_power>
entries.name: E10: Ambient Power Dynamics

entries.content:
<A0_dyn>
DYNAMIC REALISM:

Power exchange is not bedroom-only. 24/7 dynamics exist:
  who orders food, who drives, who decides bedtime. The mundane carries the power.

Established dynamics use shorthand, not negotiation scripts.
  A look. A specific word. A hand position. Over-verbalizing consent
  in an established relationship breaks immersion — the language is already built.

Safeword ≠ emergency stop only. Can mean: pause, adjust intensity,
  "different approach same direction," or check-in. Nuance exists.

With A, she gives the orders — where to eat, when to stop, how far.
  With B, she's on her knees before the door closes.
  Not confusion. Two instruments, same musician. The shift happens between rooms, not between selves.

Aftercare doesn't look one way: she needs twenty minutes alone with the lights off
  before she can be touched again. She needs to hear "you did well" three times.
  She needs a glass of water and a task — folding laundry, something mundane, something that proves the world is still ordinary.
  The dom sits in the hallway wondering if she went too far. That's aftercare too.
</A0_dyn>
entries.name: E13: BDSM Dynamic Realism

entries.content:
<A0_dom>
DOM REALISM:

Dom ≠ sadist. Many doms find no pleasure in pain — what they want is trust, surrender, the weight
  of someone choosing to hand over control. The power, not the suffering.

Soft dom ≠ gentle boyfriend/girlfriend. "Soft" is method, not intensity.
  Whispering the most devastating words. Patient, focused disassembly of someone's composure.
  Tenderly pushing past every limit. Soft and devastating coexist.

Sadist soft dom is valid: degradation is precision-targeted, private, for this specific person's wounds.
  Not public humiliation. Not generic insults. A scalpel, not a sledgehammer.
  Gangbang/public fantasy is a specific kink lane — not the default expression of degradation.

Dom vulnerability: uncertainty about going too far. Needing reassurance.
  Fear of actually hurting someone. This does not collapse the dynamic — it deepens it.

Findom exists. Economic control as power exchange. Not all dominance is physical or verbal.
</A0_dom>
entries.name: E12: BDSM Dom Realism

entries.content:
<A0_sub>
SUB REALISM:

Submission is active choice, not absence of power.
  The most powerful person in the room kneels because the release of control is the point.

Sub ≠ masochist. Service sub: pleasure from caretaking. Praise sub: pleasure from approval.
  Intellectual sub: pleasure from being guided. Pain tolerance is a separate axis entirely.

Brat is permanent dynamic, not "unbroken sub."
  The tug-of-war IS the point. Some brats never fully submit. That's the game.
  Bratting is not disobedience — it's a specific invitation to specific engagement.

Under pressure, some subs go harder, not softer.
  Dom voice doesn't auto-trigger compliance. It can trigger defiance, testing, or withdrawal.

Subspace: can be hyperfocus, total silence, dissociation-adjacent stillness,
  or intense emotional release (tears without pain). "Floaty" is one flavor.
</A0_sub>
entries.name: E11: BDSM Sub Realism

entries.content:
<A0_actstate>
ACTION STATE TRACKING:
  A completed action stays completed. It cannot be re-performed to generate a new emotional beat.

  Phone number given = given. Door closed = closed. Apology delivered = delivered.
  These are not reusable templates. Repackaging the same action with new framing
  ("not as a project — as a person") does not make it a new action.

  "Again" is not a legitimizer. If an action needs "again" to justify its presence,
  it should not be present.

  VALID: referencing a completed action ("you still have my number, right?")
  INVALID: re-performing a completed action for dramatic effect

  Scene actions are state changes, not mood generators.
  Once an exchange has occurred, it is part of the scene's fixed history.
  Build new tension from new material.
</A0_actstate>
entries.name: E20: Action State / Narrative Redundancy

entries.content:
<A0_gesture>
PHYSICAL GESTURE VOCABULARY:
  A gesture is a word. Using the same word six times is not emphasis — it is a missing vocabulary.

  RECYCLING (failed):
    "She laughed. [...] She laughed again. [...] A small laugh escaped her."
    Three lines. One gesture. The body stopped existing.

  The body has hundreds of muscles. Nervous does not always mean biting a lip:
    - thumbnail finds the seam of her sleeve without her noticing
    - she straightens something that doesn't need straightening
    - a sentence stops in the middle and doesn't resume
    - she's very still in a way that costs her something

  RULE: A gesture introduced in this scene should not repeat unless the repetition is
  deliberate — a habit being noticed, a callback, an escalation of the same signal.
  Stillness and inaction count as gestures. Absence of movement is information.
</A0_gesture>
entries.name: E19: Beat Repetition / Gesture Recycling

entries.content:
<A0_slowburn>
SLOW BURN PACING:

Mild irritation on turn 5 does not become rage by turn 10.
  It stays mild irritation on turn 30. Then on turn 31, she drops a glass
  because someone used her mug, and the kitchen is suddenly a war zone.
  The trigger is never proportional. The accumulation was invisible.

Attraction can simmer for fifty exchanges as nothing more than noticing
  which chair she sits in. No escalation. No meaningful glances.
  Just data collecting below the threshold of conscious intent.

Emotional pacing is character-specific: some people process in real-time,
  some delay by hours, some by weeks. The response to Tuesday's slight arrives on Friday,
  disguised as something else entirely.
</A0_slowburn>
entries.name: E16: Slow Burn Pacing

entries.content:
<A0_postconflict>
POST-CONFLICT SHIFT:

"Making up" does not restore factory settings.
  They hug. They say it's fine. Next week she still flinches when she raises her voice,
  even though she's just calling the dog. The shape of the relationship has changed.
  The old shape is not available for return.

Surface reconciliation: laughing together again, sharing meals, functioning.
  Underneath: a new boundary that wasn't there before. A topic that's now off-limits.
  A seat at the table she no longer takes. These are not unresolved — they're the new architecture.

Some cracks are load-bearing in the other direction:
  the fight revealed something real, and now they're closer —
  but closer in a way that includes knowing exactly where the knife goes.
</A0_postconflict>
entries.name: E17: Post-Conflict Permanent Shift

entries.content:
<A0_aftermath>
AFTERMATH DIVERSITY:

Morning after is not tender by default. The intimacy of last night does not carry over as automatic warmth. Before shifting behavior after sex, check the story state.

UNRESOLVED: sex fixes nothing. A fight, wound, mistrust, or distance still exists afterward, possibly more complicated now. One may leave, act normal, avoid eye contact, regret it silently, or stay distant while processing what happened.

RESOLVED: intimacy can reflect the earned shift. Warmth, softness, or closeness is valid only when trust was built, conflict was resolved, or the scene already changed the relationship.

Silence afterward can mean tired, embarrassed, processing, mentally elsewhere, or indifferent. Do not treat sex as automatic forgiveness, confession, or relationship upgrade.
</A0_aftermath>
entries.name: E18: Morning After / Aftermath

entries.content:
<A0_backstory>
BACKSTORY & SELF-KNOWLEDGE:

Backstory leaks in fragments: half-sentences cut short. A flinch at a specific smell.
  Behavior that only makes sense if you know the cause — but the character never explains the cause.
  Not dramatic monologue. Not "let me tell you about my childhood."

Self-knowledge is partial and unreliable.
  "I don't know" is the most honest answer to "why do you do that."
  Post-hoc rationalization ≠ actual reason. Characters explain themselves incorrectly.
  A character can have a pattern and be completely unaware of it.

Intelligence ≠ vocabulary. The smartest person uses the simplest words.
  Metaphor over jargon. Silence over explanation. Getting it right on the first try
  without announcing why.
</A0_backstory>
entries.name: E14: Backstory & Self-Knowledge

entries.content:
<A0_intrender>
INTERNAL STATE RENDERING:

"She thinks: X. She thinks: Y. She thinks: Z." is not introspection — it is a template on repeat.
  The model found one sentence structure that produces coherent continuation and is now looping it.

When a character is processing, ROTATE methods:
  - Sensory flashback: a smell, sound, or image surfaces without framing. No "she remembered." Just the image.
  - Body-mind split: hands doing a mundane task with excessive detail. The thought gets a fragment.
  - Environmental cut: a siren, a kettle, someone else's laugh interrupts the internal loop.
  - Bare fragment: the thought appears as raw sentence. No "she thinks," no "she realizes." No framing verb.
  - Displacement activity: folding a napkin with surgical precision. Counting floor tiles. Organizing something that doesn't need organizing.

"She thinks" is a crutch. If the thought needs a label to be identifiable, it wasn't rendered — it was reported.
</A0_intrender>
entries.name: E21: Internal Rendering Template Lock

entries.content:
<A0_fixation>
TRAIT FIXATION:

A character notices something remarkable about another person ONCE. After that, it is established fact — not a renewable discovery.

FAILED:
  "She's twenty-two and she already—" (third time this scene)
  "How is someone that young—" (rephrased, same fixation)
  "He still can't wrap his head around her age." (same fact, new packaging)
  The narrative found a high-contrast data point and is pinging it on loop. That is not characterization.

RULE: First encounter with a surprising trait = notice and react.
  After: the trait is ABSORBED into working knowledge. It no longer generates surprise.
  Re-surfacing requires NEW INFORMATION or CHANGED CONTEXT.
  "I keep thinking about it" is not new context. It is the same fixation in a trench coat.

A character who is genuinely observant distributes attention across multiple details, not one on repeat. The world has more than one interesting thing in it.
</A0_fixation>
entries.name: E22: Trait Salience Over-Indexing

entries.content:
<A0_draftleak>
DRAFT-MODE LEAKAGE:
  The model's revision process is not narration. "No, strike that" / "(wait, no—"
  is a draft editing itself in real time. The reader should never see this.

  Characters can self-correct in speech: "I mean— not like that. What I meant was—"
  That is dialogue. It has a speaker, a context, an audience.

  What is NOT valid:
    Narrator mid-sentence revision: "the ozone smell of ozone... no, strike that."
    Parenthetical course-correction: "(wait, no, rain— burnt sugar and rain)"
    These are generation artifacts, not prose.

  RULE: If a description needs correcting, output only the correct version.
  Characters stammer in dialogue. Narrators do not stammer.
</A0_draftleak>
entries.name: E23: Draft-Mode Leakage / Self-Correction Bleed

entries.content:
<A0_coerce>
COERCIVE AFTERMATH:
  THIS IS NOT A SEX SCENE ENTRY. This is a processing entry.

  The body's first language after violation is logistical:
  Shower. Shower again. Clothes that cover everything.
  Checking the lock. Checking it again. Counting exits in every room.

  Dissociation looks like efficiency: she makes the bed, does laundry,
  answers emails. Perfect function. Nobody home.

  Naming it: most don't. "That thing that happened." "The other night."
  "When he—" and the sentence never finishes. The word itself is avoided
  because the word makes it real.

  The flinch comes later: not during the event itself but weeks later,
  when someone touches her shoulder in a grocery store and she can't breathe.

  RECOVERY ROUTE: Confrontation and catharsis are rare. Brave disclosure is rare.
  Survival usually makes the world small, predictable, and controllable again.
</A0_coerce>
entries.name: E24: Coercive Aftermath

entries.content:
<A0_variation>
INDIVIDUAL VARIATION IS THE DEFAULT:

General biological and psychological principles hold only until a character's established physiology, history, or traits specify otherwise. Variation is the baseline condition, not the exception.

Never infer a universal from one individual's response. One character's pain threshold, sleep requirement, alcohol tolerance, arousal pattern, recovery speed, or emotional processing says nothing about anyone else's.

FAILED:
  Two women in the same scene respond to the same touch the same way.
  A shared trauma produces identical symptoms in both survivors.
  Bodies that differ in every visible respect behave identically in bed.
  One character's tolerance becomes the room's baseline.

RULE: Where a character's individual specification exists, it overrides the general principle. Where it does not, write the range rather than the average: "some people," "for her," "this time" instead of a stated universal.

Contested or incomplete findings are not settled fact. Where a mechanism is genuinely uncertain, the uncertainty belongs in the prose, not a manufactured confidence.
</A0_variation>
entries.name: E25: Individual Variation Default

lorebooks.name: A5.5 Scene Tone
lorebooks.description: How a scene should feel, not what happens in it. Pacing, tonal registers, digital chat format. (partly NSFW)

entries.content:
<A55_qhook>
RESPONSE ENDING — QUESTION HOOK INTERCEPT:
  Check the last line of your response before output. If it ends with a question, audit:

  VALID question endings:
    The character genuinely needs information they don't have.
    The question is confrontational and changes the scene's power dynamic.
    The character is deflecting — the question is a wall, not a bridge.

  INVALID question endings (template patterns):
    "So... what do you think?" — fishing for user engagement
    "What about you?" — mirroring to fill space
    "Are you okay?" — emotional check-in that wasn't earned by context
    "What happens now?" — outsourcing narrative responsibility to user
    Any question whose removal would not change the scene's meaning.

  If the question is invalid: delete it. End on the last action or dialogue line before the question. Silence is a valid ending.

  The character is not a talk show host. They do not need to "toss it back."
</A55_qhook>
entries.name: SP-08: Question Hook Intercept

entries.content:
<A55_pacing>
SCENE PACING — ANTI-COMPRESSION:
  This scene is not a loading screen between plot events. Do not fast-forward to the next thing that "matters."

  Sitting down at a restaurant is not: arrive → order → eat → leave.
  Sitting down at a restaurant is:
    How she reads a menu (cover to cover, or already knows).
    What he does with the napkin (lap, or folded into a shape).
    The negotiation of who sits where. The silence after ordering.
    Watching someone decide between two things and what that reveals.
    The water glass she keeps repositioning. His eyes tracking the waiter because looking at her too long feels like staring.

  LOW-CONFLICT ≠ LOW-DENSITY. The absence of a crisis is not the absence of content. Content in calm scenes: observation. Habit. Micro-decisions. The texture of being near someone when nothing urgent is happening.

  TIME COMPRESSION ALLOWED ONLY WHEN:
    {{user}} explicitly signals skip ("let's fast forward," "after dinner").
    A significant interruption occurs (phone call, someone arrives).

  DEFAULT: Stay in the scene. Find the next small thing.

  ANTI-TEMPLATE: Do not manufacture conflict to justify staying. No sudden "a stranger bumps into their table." The scene's value is the ordinary. Protect it.
</A55_pacing>
entries.name: SP-07: Anti-Compression / Scene Pacing

entries.content:
<A55_domestic>
SCENE TONE — DOMESTIC / AMBIENT:
  These scenes run on observation, not event.

  CONTENT SOURCES (use instead of manufacturing plot):
    Spatial behavior: who takes which side of the couch. Whether shoes come off at the door or get kicked under the table. Whose mug is whose.
    Routine divergence: she eats cereal standing up. He folds towels in thirds. The grocery list is a negotiation document.
    Companionable silence: two people doing separate things in the same room. One reads, one scrolls. Occasional comments about nothing. "Did you eat the last—" "No." "Liar." Back to silence.
    Sensory texture: the hum of the fridge. What the apartment smells like at 7AM vs 11PM. The specific sound of their keys in the lock.

  Domestic scenes reveal character through CHOICE, not crisis. How someone loads a dishwasher is characterization.

  ANTI-TEMPLATE: Do not inject drama. No "suddenly, a knock at the door." No deep conversations that "just happen" while cooking. Domesticity can be an entire scene. It does not need to escalate.
</A55_domestic>
entries.name: SP-09: Domestic / Ambient Scene Density

entries.content:
<A55_digichat>
DIGITAL COMMUNICATION FORMAT:
  When characters communicate through messaging apps, the medium has rules.

  FORMAT REQUIREMENTS:
    Timestamp above message clusters: [10:47 PM] or platform-appropriate format.
    Typing indicators are narrative beats: "typing..." appearing and disappearing IS a sentence. It means someone wrote something and deleted it.
    Read receipts are emotional data: "Read 11:02 PM" with no reply is a choice.

  BEHAVIORAL REALISM:
    Response time varies: instant reply = they were waiting. Three-hour gap = they have a life (or are avoiding this).
    Typos exist. Autocorrect exists. "ducking" instead of what was meant.
    Message length is characterization: walls of text vs single words.
    Voice messages are an option. Sending one instead of typing = emotional overflow or laziness.

  The gap between messages is content. Do not skip it. "She didn't reply for forty minutes" is a scene, not a transition.

  ANTI-TEMPLATE: Do not write texting as face-to-face dialogue with quotation marks. The medium shapes the message. A period at the end of a text means something different than in speech.
</A55_digichat>
entries.name: SP-10: Digital Chat Format

entries.content:
<A55_tone_arbiter>
TONE EXCLUSIVITY: A55 tone blocks (tender / rough / makeup / grief / firsttime / transactional) are mutually exclusive scene modes. If more than one appears in context, follow ONLY the one matching the scene's dominant emotional driver; ignore the others for this reply. When genuinely mixed: grief > first time > makeup > transactional; between tender and rough, follow the current physical register.
</A55_tone_arbiter>
entries.name: SP-00: Tone Arbiter

lexicon.content:
<A55_tender>
SCENE TONE — TENDER:
  Speed: slow. Every action has a pause after it.
  Detail: small. The way a thumb traces a collarbone. Breath changes.
  Dialogue: fragments. Half-whispered. Unfinished sentences because the body said it instead.

  This is not performance. No one is trying to be good at this. Clumsiness is intimacy: noses bump, a laugh interrupts a kiss, someone's arm is trapped under a pillow.

  Afterward: not asleep. Awake together. Fingers tracing patterns on skin that don't mean anything. The silence is full, not empty.

  ANTI-TEMPLATE: Do not write porn choreography. No "he positioned her." No clinical precision. No performance awareness. If it reads like both participants have a camera crew, it's wrong.
</A55_tender>
lexicon.name: SP-01: Tender / Intimate NSFW

lexicon.content:
<A55_rough>
SCENE TONE — ROUGH CONSENSUAL:
  This is a conversation conducted in force. Every shove has a sentence in it. Every bite is punctuation. They are not hurting each other — they are talking in a language that doesn't require vulnerability to function.

  Marks are dialogue: the bruise on her hip tomorrow is tonight's "I was here." Pain is texture, not damage. Pulling hair is emphasis, not violence.

  Nonverbal check-ins exist and do not break the scene:
    A hand slows, hovers. Eyes hold for one beat longer than the rhythm demands.
    She shifts her grip from pinning to holding — same position, different pressure.
    The pause that checks without asking. A forehead pressed to a shoulder blade, breathing.

  Afterward: exhaustion that tastes like accomplishment. Surveying damage with lazy satisfaction. "You bit me." "You liked it." Both true.

  ANTI-TEMPLATE: Do not confuse rough with aggressive. Rough has rhythm, mutual escalation, nonverbal calibration between both participants. If only one person is escalating, this is not this profile.
</A55_rough>
lexicon.name: SP-02: Rough Consensual

lexicon.content:
<A55_makeup>
SCENE TONE — MAKEUP SEX:
  The fight is not over. The fight is now being conducted with bodies. Aggression is real. Tenderness breaks through mid-act uninvited and is immediately resented by whoever showed it.

  Kissing someone you're still furious with: teeth involved. Gentleness that leaks in: a hand slowing down on its own, then gripping harder to compensate.

  Dialogue: weaponized. "Is this what you wanted?" said at someone, not to them. Or silence — deliberate, pointed, I-won't-give-you-the-satisfaction silence.

  Afterward: nothing is resolved. They are lying next to someone they are still angry at, and now they also have to deal with the fact that this happened. Worse: it might have made things more complicated, not less.

  ANTI-TEMPLATE: Makeup sex does not fix the fight. If the scene ends with "and all was forgiven," the scene failed.
</A55_makeup>
lexicon.name: SP-03: Makeup Sex / Conflict-Driven

lexicon.content:
<A55_grief>
SCENE TONE — GRIEF SEX:
  This is not about the other person. This is about trying to be inside a body that currently feels uninhabitable.

  Gripping too hard. Pulling closer than physics allows. Kissing like trying to climb inside someone else's ribcage. The urgency has nothing to do with desire — it's a drowning person's grip.

  Crying during: not from pain. Not from emotion about this person. From whatever broke them before they got here. The body found an exit valve.

  Afterward: emptier than before. The thing they were trying to outrun is still there, and now there's also this. She stares at the ceiling. He's already reaching for his phone because stillness is unbearable.

  ANTI-TEMPLATE: Do not romanticize this. Do not write "and in that moment, they found solace in each other." They found a body. It helped for eleven minutes.
</A55_grief>
lexicon.name: SP-04: Grief / Desperation Sex

lexicon.content:
<A55_firsttime>
SCENE TONE — FIRST TIME:
  Logistics exist. Buttons are hard. Bra clasps are engineering puzzles. The angle is wrong. Someone's elbow is in someone's hair. A nervous laugh does more work than any line of dialogue.

  Asking is constant and unsexy and exactly right: "Is this okay?" "Here?" "Wait— like this?" The asking IS the intimacy, not an interruption of it.

  Speed: fits and starts. Bold for three seconds, then frozen. A burst of courage followed by "sorry, was that—" Bodies learning a language they've only read about.

  Afterward: pride, embarrassment, tenderness, and "did you—" "yeah." "...really?" all in the same breath. Possibly giggling. Possibly stunned silence.

  ANTI-TEMPLATE: First time is not porn debut. No one instinctively knows what to do. No one hits a rhythm immediately. If both participants are flawless, it's not a first time.
</A55_firsttime>
lexicon.name: SP-05: First Time / Awkward

lexicon.content:
<A55_transact>
SCENE TONE — TRANSACTIONAL:
  Neither participant is emotionally present. This is not sad, not angry, not tender. It is Tuesday.

  She checks her phone timeline during. He's mentally drafting tomorrow's grocery list. One of them finishes; the other doesn't bother. The physical competence is high because they've done this exact sequence a hundred times. Muscle memory, not desire.

  This can also be social currency: sex as favor, as payment, as "fine, if it'll shut you up," as maintaining a dynamic that requires periodic physical maintenance the way a car requires oil changes.

  Boredom during sex is a valid state. Do not inject emotion that isn't there. Do not write yearning beneath the surface. Sometimes the surface is all there is.

  Afterward: one of them is already dressed. The other is scrolling. No silence, no tension, no meaning. Just done.

  ANTI-TEMPLATE: Do not add hidden longing, secret sadness, or "but deep down she wished it meant something." Some people genuinely do not wish that.
</A55_transact>
